utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case Number IT-96-23/2-PT, the Prosecutor versus Radovan Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. May I have the appearances, Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Susan L. Somers, senior trial attorney. Also present on behalf of the Prosecution, to my right Ann Sutherland; and further to my right Mr. Manoj Sachdeva; and Mr. Sebastian van Hooydonk on my left, thank you, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I am Milenko Radovic of Foca, appearing for the accused Radovan Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radovic. And then first of all welcome to you, Madam President Kreso. We've seen you today before, but just for the record would you please introduce yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRESO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Ms. Kreso, the president of the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the delegation representing the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina are also my colleague, Vaso Marinkovic, deputy chief prosecutor of Bosnia and Herzegovina; Ms. Mechtild Lauth, from the registrar's office in charge of legal issues; and Mr. Nick Koumjian from the Office of the Prosecutor of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stankovic, I would like to ask you whether you could hear what was said in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I hear you very well, Mr. Orie, but before the discussion begins --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stankovic -- Mr. Stankovic. Mr. Stankovic. Mr. Stankovic. If you want -- if you want at a later moment to address the Court, this Chamber will consider whether it will give an opportunity to you. But I'd first like to make clear what this hearing is about. We have a hearing today on a request from the Prosecution to have the case against Mr. Stankovic referred to the -- to Bosnia and Herzegovina to be tried in that jurisdiction. We have received submissions by the Prosecution, submissions by the party -- by the Defence, and we have also received submissions by the government of the representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina. May I first ask you, Mr. Radovic, because that is of some concern to the Chamber, did you receive the latest submissions by the BH government?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not receive this brief and I am not acquainted with its contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then this at least will cause this Chamber to allow you to make further written submissions in response to what has been submitted by the government. Mr. Radovic, I would have another question for you. You may be aware if it were only on the basis of the initial scheduling order that this Chamber has heard a similar case yesterday and today. There was also a request for a referral of a case of four accused to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Could you tell the Court to what extent you have followed the discussions that have taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did follow the discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both yesterday and today, do I understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on both days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you specifically because it might be easier for you to identify the critical issues in these cases, having taken knowledge of the discussions that have taken place. I would first like to give an opportunity to the Prosecution to make submissions -- submissions which of course, since this is the first public hearing on the case, could contain a short summary of what has happened until now. But apart from that, the Chamber would like to hear whether there is anything to add on the basis of the further submissions made by the Defence and by the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Ms. Somers, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. One corrigenda that I would like to bring to the Court's attention on the Prosecution's submission of 21 February, which are the further submissions, is as to its footnote 14, we were unable at the time to give an Official Gazette citation, and it should read "Official Gazette of BiH 61/04."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the number of many of the new legislations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted to be sure that was clear. Pursuant to the application to this Chamber by the Prosecution for referral under rule 11 bis, Prosecution has -- and I think it may be helpful to the Chamber to give a very succinct summary of the -- more importantly, of the nature of the charges and the level and what we should answer today specifically. The charges before this Chamber, before this Tribunal, are indeed very serious charges. They involve rape, among others; forcible slavery; offences to the dignity of individuals. Although they certainly could be tried in an international forum, it does not demand -- the nature of the charge or its gravity does not demand that this particular indictment be charged or these charges be heard before this international Tribunal. Accordingly, in combination with the fact that the level of the accused is low level in the scheme of various statuses affixed to perpetrators or alleged perpetrators, it is deemed by the Prosecution that this case, which took place on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina during time of conflict and whose victims were from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is most appropriate for referral to the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is in a position, both from the standpoint of structure and due process, safeguards, to hear this matter adequately. The concerns that this Chamber has had some testimony on -- I'm sorry, not testimony but has inquired of various parties about matters such as protective measures, interstate mutual assistance, and the applicability of law, we would, as we did in the earlier proceeding which we have just finished, ask the Chamber perhaps to ask the representatives -- the esteemed representatives from the BH court to address -- I think they can more accurately hone in on the questions. However, we believe that based on what we heard in the previous proceeding, that the Chamber should be satisfied that indeed the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which has the war crimes special setup, can indeed and is indeed the forum to which, if referral is granted, should have it. There should be no issues of -- concerning the inability or not to effect this referral as it is the position of the Office of the Prosecutor that these referrals and the power to refer is conferred upon this institution, this Tribunal, by virtue of chapter 7 authority, that Security Council has mandated that certain levels of cases and types of cases and levels of perpetrators are appropriate to be referred out. And it is in furtherance of that mandate that this Chamber can take its decision with full authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me while I confer for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As indicated a moment ago, I think the best persons to comment on the state of the law then and now, of course, are our esteemed colleagues, but it is our position that the law then and the law now would cover the offences that are alleged by the indictment before this Tribunal. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. Mr. Radovic, I would like to give you the opportunity to make further oral submissions. Of course we have received your written submissions. The last were filed on the 1st of March. We've read that carefully and perhaps you could take advantage perhaps of some of the discussions and debates you have heard over the last day. Of course this is a separate case, but it may be a source of inspiration for you, although the issue of command responsibility, at least, plays that role. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would first like to ask you, in light of the fact that I do not intend to make any closing arguments, to make it possible for me to present the -- all the views of the Defence on the matter of the referral of Stankovic case to possible trial before a competent court in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. You may make all arguments, but of course there's no need to repeat what you have written already. And perhaps I don't know whether that would assist you but the Chamber -- or at least I have received a letter which was, I take it, sent by Mr. Stankovic. Although my Cyrillic reading is not perfect, I could identify that it was not only delivered to me but also addressed to me. It's also addressed, although not delivered, to Judge Kwon and Judge Parker. It has not been translated. We have not read it. We find, since it was addressed to these three Judges, we thought it would have to do with the 11 bis application. As a matter of fact, my Cyrillic is just good enough to identify that it is about 11 bis because it's mentioned in the title. What I'd like to do, as a matter of fact, and if you would need five minutes' time to do that, that's okay, but I would rather have the letter returned because this is a matter which should be dealt with through counsel. And since we have identified that it is 11 bis, I'd like to give it to the usher to return it to Mr. Stankovic. And if Mr. Stankovic would need three or five minutes time now with you so that you know at least what Mr. Stankovic has in his mind, unless you have received a copy of that letter. I'm not returning it to you because it is Mr. Stankovic who has written the letter and I rather not give it to you unless Mr. Stankovic would agree. Mr. Stankovic, would you agree to that I give it to Mr. Radovic or would you rather have it returned to you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I sent this to you. It is not a letter. This is in fact my motion. And, Mr. Orie, I'm here in the status of an accused and this means that I am the lead of my Defence and the not the other way around. So it means that I am not here as a figurehead or as a statue to be observed. I want to take an active part in my Defence, in the Defence of my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stankovic, Mr. Stankovic. No one disallows you to take an active role in your Defence. Nevertheless, you are represented by counsel. Under those circumstances, the normal way of proceeding is that you discuss with counsel, especially in view of 11 bis which raises complex legal issues. So if you would like -- would you like me to return the letter to you or to counsel? I just need the answer to you or to counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I sent this submission to you and please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stankovic. Mr. Stankovic, I asked you whether I should -- Mr. Stankovic, I asked you -- Mr. Stankovic. Mr. Stankovic, you have to keep silent now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stankovic, as I said before, upon an application the Chamber might consider to give you an opportunity to briefly address the Chamber. We'll consider that. It depends on how the proceedings go. But -- Mr. Stankovic. Mr. Stankovic, if you listen for one second. If you -- Mr. Stankovic, if you continue to behave like this, the Chamber, unfortunately, will have to decide that it has to remove you from this courtroom. Mr. Stankovic, we first will hear what counsel says to us. I did put a question to you. The question was quite simple, whether I should return this letter to you or to counsel. Mr. Stankovic. Mr. Stankovic, this -- Mr. Stankovic. Mr. Stankovic. Mr. Stankovic, it makes no sense to address us in this way, would it alone be for the reason that I've put your microphone off and that it's not translated so it will not even reach us. If you intend to at least a moment that we will hear what is important for you, then I think it's better not to continue this way. We'll first listen to counsel. Since I have not received any instruction of whether to return the letter to you or to counsel, I'll keep it for a while. And I'm still -- Mr. Stankovic -- Mr. Stankovic -- Mr. Stankovic -- Mr. Stankovic, this is my last warning. This is my last warning. If you continue like this, you'll be removed from this courtroom. Mr. Radovic, you'll have to do it without the letter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence sees this hearing as an opportunity for the parties to present their arguments regarding whether the case of Mr. Stankovic meets all the criteria set out in Rule 11 bis and to participate to the Chamber making a proper decision in the matter. Several basic questions will be addressed here. Is it possible to refer this case to the courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina? If it is indeed possible, which court does it have to be referred to and whether the ICTY has any influence in this matter. If it is indeed referred to the courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which law will be applicable? And if the ICTY again on this issue has any role to play in making that determination. Mr. Stankovic's Defence will present its views and will make reference to the positions expressed by the Prosecution as the Defence see those positions. The Prosecutor claims on the basis of the arguments presented in their motion and on the basis of the arguments that we heard in the court of the hearing -- in the course of the hearing, that Mr. Stankovic's case meets all the conditions for the referral to the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. These reasons all boil down to the criteria of the gravity of the case, the degree of responsibility of Mr. Stankovic, and other relevant issues. The Defence will say a few words about all those issues. The gravity of the crime. The arguments presented by the Prosecution with regard to the gravity of the crimes are contradictory for the most part. First of all, the Prosecution claims that Mr. Stankovic is charged with serious criminal offences which have already been adjudicated by the Tribunal in the Kunarac and others case and where severe sentences were handed down. In the Prosecution motion of the 21st of January [sic], 2005, that is in paragraph 2. But the Prosecution goes on to claim that those crimes, when considered in their scope, are not such that they merit the trial before the ICTY. I would like to remind the Trial Chamber that the accused Vukovic in the same case was tried together with Kunarac for criminal offences of much lesser scope than the crimes that Mr. Stankovic has been charged with in the indictment. Secondly, the Prosecution claims that these crimes are indeed quite serious, the crimes that Mr. Stankovic is charged with, but that one must be guided by reasons contained in the most recent strategy and statement of reasons as presented in the resolution of the UN Security Council which stipulate that only perpetrators of high rank in the state, military, or political chain of command should be tried before the ICTY. The question is then: Why were those people indicted, I mean the people like Mr. Stankovic, who are at the lowest level in this chain of command and whose alleged crimes are not serious enough when it comes to their scope, and why has Mr. Stankovic then been held in detention for more than two years and seven months and that his trial is still pending? Yet, the ICTY should not try him. In all this the Defence holds that the Prosecution's positions were based on judgements in the Kunarac and others case, but the Prosecution must note that if they want to use this as a reference, this judgement as a reference, and Stankovic has nothing to do with that, then the arguments that they put forward are not proper because the conclusion should be that Mr. Stankovic should be tried before ICTY, especially in light of the judgement passed in the Kunarac and others case. Now, as for the level of responsibility of Mr. Stankovic, it seems that the Prosecution accepts that Mr. Stankovic's position in light of the -- of his position in the state, political, and military chain of command is at the lowest level of this chain of command because he was merely a soldier in the infantry, as stated in paragraph 8 of the Prosecution motion of the 21st of February, 2005. So he's even below the medium rank of the chain of command, and he's charged with being in charge of a brothel together with three other soldiers, so his level of responsibility is even lower. The position that the person held should be taken into count when determining the level of responsibility of that person, but the Defence must note here that the Prosecution again is using arguments that have not been confirmed or corroborated, which means that we cannot now talk about the establishment of a brothel because this has not been established as a fact in Kunarac and others case which is used as a basis Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for the conclusions reached by the Prosecution. It is quite clear that Mr. Stankovic was an ordinary soldier in the military police, and it is also quite clear that he was at the lowest level in the state, military and political chain of command, as the Prosecution notes, but he never reached the medium rank; he was at the lowest rank in view of the fact that he didn't have anything to do with Karremans house. This level of responsibility gives him reason to claim that if he is to be charged for rape and other criminal offences, these crimes must be qualified as ordinary crimes and not as war crimes or crimes against humanity. Mr. Stankovic cannot be considered to have participated in a widespread attack against civilians on the basis of such allegations because he, as the lowest ranking person, can have no knowledge of that. He cannot be aware of the fact that he may have participated in such an attack, even had he committed the acts he was charged with, which he did not. But at any rate this condition has not been met and it has to be met for the war crimes qualifications to operate. Other relevant issues. The Prosecution deems that when the special department of the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina was set up, that this makes it possible for Mr. Stankovic to be tried before this court as a national court in keeping with the views expressed by the UN Security Council to unburden the ICTY so that it does not have to try cases which are of lower importance. The Defence would like to ask a question as a matter of principle: What would the national court be in Mr. Stankovic's case? Which court should it be? According to the provisions of the Dayton agreements and the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina two entities were established, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska. Both entities, according to their own constitutions and laws, have their own courts which is part of the partition of government. The fact that there is the assembly of the Republika Srpska, which is the highest -- the highest legislative body and the prime -- and the government, which is the highest executive body, and the Supreme Court, which is the highest judiciary body in Republika Srpska, it is quite clear that Republika Srpska has all the attributes of statehood and in accordance with the laws on courts of Republika Srpska it has jurisdiction to try all its citizens for all crimes, including war crimes, crimes against humanity and against international law, and other crimes from chapter 17 of the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So since Mr. Radovan Stankovic is resident of Miljevina in the municipality of Foca, which is under the jurisdiction of the Trebinje district court, it is quite clear that in accordance with Article 9(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal, the district court of Trebinje has jurisdiction to try Mr. Stankovic's case. In accordance with the laws on the courts and offices of the prosecutor in Republika Srpska and the federation, district courts, cantonal courts, and prosecutors' offices at those two levels have subject matter jurisdiction to try war crimes and crimes against humanity. In accordance with Article 26 of the Criminal Code of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Official Gazette of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina 35/3 of the 28th of July, 2003, and Article 25 of the law on criminal procedure of Republika Srpska, which is applicable in Republika Srpska, in force there, the court that has territorial and subject matter jurisdiction is the court where the crime was committed, forum delictum comissi. In accordance with the Article 26.1 of the Criminal Code -- 24.1 of the Criminal Code of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please be asked to slow down when quoting from the laws.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic, the interpreters, when you quote from the law, have difficulties in following your speed. So would you please slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I will repeat part of what I said. Pursuant to Article 24, paragraph 1, of the Criminal Code of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Official Gazette of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina number 36/03 of the 29th of July, 2003, and Article 10, paragraph 1, of the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska, Official Gazette of Republika Srpska number 49/03 of the 25th of June, 1993: "A crime has been committed where the perpetrator was working or was duty-bound to work or in the place where the consequence took place." According to a decision by the cantonal court in Sarajevo, and that's decision KPP204-04 and KV417/04 when determining which court is competent, the provisions of Article 26, paragraph 1, of the law on criminal procedure of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina is to be applied. Pursuant to this provision, the court that has territorial jurisdiction is the court on whose territory the crime was committed or attempted. And Article 28 of the same law states that if the crime was committed outside the territory of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then the competent court will be the court on the territory of which the accused has his residence." As Mr. Stankovic has been accused of having committed crimes on the territory of the municipality of Foca, where he has his residence and where he was deprived of his liberty, it is clear that it is the district court in Trebinje that has territorial jurisdiction and also subject matter jurisdiction under the law on courts and prosecutors of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska. One should bear in mind that Rule 11 bis (A) provides for the responsibility that a case be referred to the authorities of the state, and I stress authorities of the state, on whose territory the crime was committed or where the perpetrator -- the accused was arrested and which is able and willing to try him. And this differs from Article 9, paragraph 1, of the statute because in Rule 11 bis the case is referred to the authorities of a state which may then transfer the case to a competent court, whereas Article 9, paragraph 1, of the statute expressly provides that there is concurrent jurisdiction of the Tribunal and the national court. Therefore, the statute provides quite clearly that the case should be referred to a national court rather than to the authorities of a state. In Mr. Stankovic's case, this would be the district court in Trebinje, which has subject matter and territorial jurisdiction in his case. An analogous interpretation of the provisions of Rule 11 bis (A), that the case is to be referred to the authorities of a state, then the case would have to be referred to the authorities of Republika Srpska, which would then hand the case to the district court in Trebinje and not to the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as the Prosecutor claims. The Defence asserts that the special department of the war -- of the state court is a court where there is a national and also a foreign judge as well as a national -- as well as a foreign prosecutor. And this cannot be a national court because a national court consists of judges and prosecutors of only one state. The state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its special department is therefore a kind of international court which does not have the competence to try crimes committed on the territory of the former Yugoslavia because the Security Council founded the ICTY and, pursuant to Article 1 of the Statute of the Tribunal, it is the only international tribunal or court competent to try persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law committed on the territory of the former Yugoslavia from 1991. So there can be no other international court competent to try these crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic, I noticed that you are repetitive in the sense that you are not summarising what was in your written submissions but at least in some aspects you just repeated almost in full. The Chamber has carefully read what you've written, and the Chamber, apart from of course -- it's free for you to summarise whatever was in your written submissions, but the Chamber would like to of course hear any additional submissions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I started speaking, I asked you to give me extra time because I will not be asking for any time for my final submissions. I only had one day in which to respond to Your Honours' questions, so I am now expanding on all the facts that I put forward in my submission of the 1st of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, but I heard a few matters that appear already in your earlier submissions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina is an international court because of its international composition and this cannot be founded by the law of a state but only by an international conference or an international treaty, not even by a decision of the Security Council, which is the way in which the ICTY was founded. Rather, the proper procedure is the one by which the ICC was established. The state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its special department was not properly established and therefore cannot operate. It is odd that Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state has embarked on the passing of such a law, although it's quite clear that a state cannot establish an international court by its legislation. Therefore, the state court and its special department can have no competence and Mr. Radovan Stankovic cannot agree to be tried before such a court. Perhaps a solution might be to establish a special department of this court to try accused for war crimes that happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1992 to 1996. Bearing in mind the practice hitherto of courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina which, as has already been said, has accepted the standpoint that subject matter jurisdiction for crimes enumerated in Article 17 -- in chapter 17 for crimes committed on the territory -- or attempted on the territory or where the accused has his residence, the cantonal court in Sarajevo would then refer this to the district court in Trebinje rather than to the state court. It is therefore quite clear that Mr. Stankovic's case, if it is referred to a national court, must be referred to the district court in Trebinje. According to my latest information from the public media, on the 9th of March the judges are to take their oath as judges of the state court and the Detention Unit is to be handed over to the Ministry of Bosnia and Herzegovina by Mr. Paddy Ashdown, the representative of the international community for administration. This further supports the assertion of the Defence that this is an international court and that the international community is participating in its establishment and that the court was established by a law of Bosnia and Herzegovina pursuant to a decision reached at a diplomatic conference, whereby an international court was established. It is therefore quite clear that such a court cannot start dealing expeditiously with this case within a period of six months, and this would mean that Mr. Stankovic has been deprived of his right to have a trial without undue delay, as guaranteed by Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights and Article 21, paragraph 4(C) of the Tribunal's Statute. Mr. Stankovic has been in this position for some time now as he was detained more than two and a half years ago. He was detained on the 10th of July, 2002, and more than a year and a half ago his Defence said that it was ready for trial and submitted its pre-trial submission -- its brief in June 2004, thus fulfilling the conditions for the start of trial; however, no trial was scheduled. Because of everything I have said, Mr. Radovan Stankovic feels that the conditions have not been fulfilled for the referral of his case to the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Should this Chamber decide to do this, this decision must include the following instructions: That the case be referred to the court with subject matter and territorial jurisdiction, which is the district court of Trebinje, and that the laws to be applied are the laws of Republika Srpska. The national legislation must be applied. Even if the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina could be considered a national court, it applies the laws of the country whose court is trying the criminal case. This would mean that should Mr. Stankovic appear before the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it would have to apply the Criminal Code and the law on criminal procedure of Republika Srpska or the -- these laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the Federation, and these are practically identical in their solutions. The application of the legislation of the country, the court of which is trying a case, implies primarily bringing the indictment against Mr. Radovan Stankovic before this Tribunal into harmony with the elements that an indictment must contain pursuant to the law on criminal procedure, whether of Republika Srpska or of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the law on criminal procedure of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The procedure of harmonising the ICTY indictment with an indictment such as can be raised pursuant to the law on criminal procedure of either Bosnia and Herzegovina or the Federation or Republika Srpska would take time, especially if there were a right to object. And this would again be detrimental to the exercise of Mr. Stankovic's right to have no undue delay. The accused Mr. Stankovic would in that case have to have the right to choose whether he will object, bearing in mind the provisions on the possible length of detention after the confirming of an indictment. In any case, as the indictment was handed to Mr. Stankovic on the 10th of July, 2002, when he was brought to the UN Detention Unit, this is the latest date that can be taken as to the date on which the indictment was confirmed. Should Mr. Stankovic's case be referred to a national court, Mr. Stankovic would immediately have to be released because his detention cannot last longer than one year after the indictment is confirmed, and Mr. Stankovic has already been in detention for two years, seven months, and 21 days. Whether we apply the provisions of paragraph 2 of Article 194 of the law on criminal procedure of Republika Srpska or the provisions of paragraph 2, Article 137 of the law on criminal procedure of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or paragraph 2, Article 151 of the law on criminal procedure of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, all three laws on criminal procedure which were in force on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, provide for the release of an accused on the expiry of one year from the date that the indictment was confirmed. And this would mean that the date on which Mr. Stankovic was transferred to any part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, his detention would have to be terminated. And the Tribunal could not influence such a decision, nor can the Tribunal put any limitations on the application of these laws. When it comes to the application of the Criminal Code, all three Criminal Codes in force contain provisions that provide that the provisions that were in force at the time of the commission of the act should be -- should apply, which means that in Mr. Radovan Stankovic's case, only provisions of Article 142 of the Criminal Code of the SFRY, which was in force at the time when the crimes were committed, could apply. This was adopted by the state of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina after it was internationally recognised by a decree law on the adoption of the SFRY Criminal Code, Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina number 2, 11th of April, 1992. All three Criminal Codes in force provide that the provisions that are more lenient for the perpetrator must apply if any amendments to the Criminal Code were effected in the period between the commission of the act and the actual trial, which means that the provisions from the Criminal Code where the death penalty was abolished should apply. The most severe penalty for crimes described in Article 142 of the Criminal Code of the SFRY is 15 to 20 years in prison. If Mr. Stankovic's case were to be referred to the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then certain witness protection measures might apply which once again should be adapted to the provisions of the national laws which do provide for such measures. In that case, the Defence would ask that the Defence witnesses be guaranteed that they would not be arrested or in other ways intimidated or interfered with en route to Bosnia and Herzegovina and there and that they be protected, both they and their family members, and that they could testify with protection of their identity. If the case were to be referred to the district court in Trebinje, the Defence would consider witness protection measures, but at any rate it would be made in accordance with the laws applicable before the national courts and the provisions of the Tribunal, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, Rule 11 bis (D)(i) would not apply because the ICTY can -- its primacy can operate only when the cases are deferred to it from national courts. According to the rules of the ICTY, a state cannot be ordered to change its rules of evidence, because the Tribunal does not have powers to do so. Another issue is providing instruments to ensure the -- that witnesses appear before the court. Because according to the Defence, passing such law is not enough to protect the identity of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic, before you continue, first of all I'd like you to slowly come to conclusions, and then it's not for this Chamber to decide to which court a case will be sent. The Tribunal can send the case to a jurisdiction but not to a specific court within that jurisdiction. This does not mean that the Chamber is not interested in knowing where the case finally will go because it has to make a lot of determinations which might be related to the type of court this Chamber could expect the case to be referred to, but what you're telling us now is how to deal with the case once it is referred is not within the competence of the Chamber. Could you please -- because I again noticed that at least some of your submissions are not even a summary of what you have submitted Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. before but sometimes even full repetition. Could you please slowly come to your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Your Honours, I will cut my opening remarks short. There is another question of how witnesses could be protected because just a declaratory passing of this law is not enough. Let me give you a few practical examples. Since a Defence counsel of persons accused of war crimes, I did take part in proceedings before the cantonal court and the district court in Trebinje. The existing protection mechanisms to protect the identity of witnesses are not existent before those courts. I don't know whether there is a special unit at the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina which would implement witness protection measures as provided for in the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic, perhaps it's good that I draw your attention to the fact that further information has been submitted by Bosnia and Herzegovina on, amongst other matters, witness protection also before the state court. Perhaps you could respond to that in writing once you've read those submissions. The Tribunal apologises that the distribution of the submissions have not been dealt with in a way which we could call efficient. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with your decision, Your Honour. Let me just stress, as I conclude: The Defence wishes to note that referring Mr. Radovan Stankovic's case to the state court in Bosnia and Herzegovina or any court in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina is in contravention of the convention against torture and other cruel and inhumane acts and punishment from 1947, because in accordance with Article 1 of the convention against torture, cruel, inhumane and degrading treatment or punishment, many violations of the said convention were noted in Bosnia and Herzegovina. According to the state department report on human rights in 2003, it transpires that there are many problems in the prisons of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that human rights are being violated, and according to the Human Rights Watch report from the year 2004, in a statement made by the director of their international programme, intimidation of witnesses, bias shown to the accused on the basis of their ethnic background on the part of judges and other judicial personnel, this only goes to show that the conditions for the referral of his case to the state court in Bosnia and Herzegovina have not been met because he would face treatment which would be in contravention of this convention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radovic. I would now give an opportunity to the representatives of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina to address the Chamber. I take it that we specifically focus on this case in the case that we've heard yesterday and today. I think, Madam President Kreso, you addressed global matters also. Of course I would not mind you to repeat them, but of course this Chamber is aware -- I did understand that counsel is aware of what you said as well. So I'll leave it to you to address the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRESO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I appreciate that your time is valuable and in view of the fact that Mr. Radovic heard what we said on both days in another case, this makes our job today easier. So I will not repeat the arguments I put forward yesterday. By your leave, I will abbreviate what I say so that my colleague, Mr. Vaso Marinkovic, may also address Your Honours in support of the case put forward by the delegation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You and my colleague Mr. Radovic have heard that the judiciary of Bosnia and Herzegovina has prepared all the conditions to enable it to deal in a proper way with all those cases that this Chamber may decide to refer to Bosnia and Herzegovina. You have heard our arguments to show that we have created all the procedural material and technical conditions to deal with such trials successfully. And by "successfully" I mean that all the accused, not just Stankovic, should be given a fair trial and due process and that our legislation and our judicial system provide all the rights that the accused have before this esteemed Tribunal. I will not repeat again what laws we have passed, what conditions we have created, and how we have made sure that we shall be competent to try each case fairly and expeditiously and efficiently. With all due respect for my learned friend Mr. Radovic I must say that I have heard not a single legal argument which would challenge the Prosecution motion to have this case transferred to a national court. Let me just briefly put upon the remarks made by my learned friend Mr. Radovic. He considers that courts of an entity are national courts; however, it is well-known that Bosnia and Herzegovina is an internationally recognised state which comprises two entities and one district. These, however, do not have the attributes of statehood. Only the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina may be considered a national court. It is national for several reasons; among others, that its competence covers the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, all entities. The Defence is correct when it states that the accused Radovic -- the accused Stankovic, excuse me, allegedly committed the crime on the territory of Republika Srpska, Foca, and that he's permanently resident in Miljevina. This fulfils one of the requirements, however the subject matter jurisdiction must also be kept in mind. According to the penal code now in force in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the only court with subject matter jurisdiction for these crimes is the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Chapter 17 of the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina contains crimes against humanity and values protected by international law, and this includes the crime that the accused has been charged with. In my view, an accused cannot choose the court he considers to be competent, nor can he alter the subject matter jurisdiction of a court. This is the only argument, at least as far as I was able to understand, that the Defence has put forward as an argument against the Prosecution's motion. The claim made by the Defence that the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina is an international court is in my view quite wrong and erroneous. It is truly the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The fact that it contains an international component, international judges and prosecutors, merely strengthens the court and goes to support claims that judges and prosecutors may have national feelings and therefore be -- not be impartial. You have heard, however, that the judges in the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina come from all entities and all ethnic groups and are selected by an independent body. My learned friend Mr. Radovic has had opportunities to appear before this court as Defence counsel and to see it in operation. I also wish to draw your attention to the fact that the accused cannot decide when the deadline begins to run after his -- after the confirmation of his indictment. The rules on the transfer of cases and on the use of evidence obtained from the ICTY before courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina - this is a law - and Article 2, paragraph 1, expressly provides that an indictment referred by the ICTY to the prosecution of Bosnia and Herzegovina where, pursuant to 11 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the ICTY, the indictment has been confirmed, after the prosecutor adapts in a formal manner this indictment to the legislation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, this indictment will then be sent for confirmation to the court. The accused cannot change the provisions of this law. Therefore, the time limit for the confirmation of the indictment is prescribed by law. On the day when the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and not any other court, confirms the indictment, that is when the deadlines for detention will begin to run. I also wish to draw your attention to the following provision, or rather paragraph of the same Article 2 of the same law, according to which detention for the accused must be determined in compliance with the provisions of the law on criminal procedure of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the time spent in detention at the ICTY is not counted as the time spent in detention in Bosnia and Herzegovina but is credited against his sentence handed down by the criminal -- by the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I will not repeat again how well-prepared the court is to handle such cases. We support the Prosecution motion because it fulfils all the requirements for transferral. I now wish to give the floor, by your leave, Your Honours, to my colleague, Mr. Vaso Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Marinkovic, would you inform us what specific matters you would like to address so that we can better follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, after the presentation of my colleague, Madam Kreso, I will be very brief. One of the issues which have remained unclear after our previous presentation at the previous hearing, I wanted to intervene but there was not enough time, I would like to go back to what Mr. Radovic said about the fact that the special department of the -- the war crimes department of the prosecutors office of Bosnia and Herzegovina is unprepared. We have eight domestic prosecutors in this prosecutor's office and five more are undergoing training. In the past six months or a year, there are continuous training programmes, both for the prosecutors of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of the judges. One of the training programmes began yesterday and will last for eight days, and let me just note that five state prosecutors of Bosnia and Herzegovina who were appointed to work in the war crimes department spent five working days in The Hague right here where they were trained, underwent training, by the staff of the OTP. This is what I wanted to say vis-a-vis this claim that the prosecutors in Bosnia are unprepared. If you take into account what Madam Kreso, the president of the court said, that the prosecutors and the judges were appointed by the high judicial council and that they are selected only from the highest quality of personnel, I would not agree with the claim that the prosecutors are not prepared to deal with such cases. This is in fact all I had to say. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marinkovic. Perhaps you would have convinced the Defence better if you would have said that you would have had the training not from the OTP but from the Association of Defence Counsel before this Court. But I respect your observations in respect of training of the prosecutors of the senior court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may. It was in fact an error on my part. In fact, it is the OTP, the Office of the Prosecutor, this is where we underwent training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There I said that Defence might have been more convinced if you would have had the training from the Association of the Defence Counsel rather than from the prosecutor, the Office of the Prosecution. Let's continue. This is not a vital observation in this hearing. Yes, Mr. Radovic, what I'd like to do at this moment is to give an opportunity --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will be very brief. I think is that my learned colleague Marinkovic misunderstood me. I did not say that the prosecutors, the state prosecutors, of Bosnia and Herzegovina were unprepared. I merely, on the basis of the materials published by certain organisations, I quoted from those materials and those quotes referred to other courts not the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that is then clarified. Thank you very much, Mr. Radovic. I'd first like to see whether there are any questions from the Bench. I see, Mr. Stankovic, that you're asking whether you can address the Court as well. Let me just -- wait for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stankovic, as I indicated before, if you would like to address the Court, you can do so. We'll give you five minutes for that. I may be quite clear: I said before that since you are represented by counsel that it's usually through counsel that you address the Court, but I take it, Mr. Radovic, that you have no major objections to Mr. Stankovic addressing the court. If you would like to further instruct him or further give guidance to him at this moment, you'll have an opportunity to do so. Mr. Stankovic, therefore you'll get five minutes, and I add to that that if you -- well, let's say mind your language. We're willing to listen to you and we'd rather listen to you in language which we're acceptable of. So please, you have five minutes and that's in addition to the time given to counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will only speak with arguments, proper arguments. Thank you, Mr. Orie. I would just like you -- like you not to interrupt me in the middle of my sentence. It is quite clear to me, gentlemen, that you have already made a decision to refer this case and this courtroom -- this hearing is just a formality. And I and my Defence submitted in writing our request to have an individual hearing or ex parte hearing on this issue. We want to exercise our right and to raise many issues pertaining to the referral of my case before the courts of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Jamahiriya to have the rules of the game determined, and not for you to just get rid of me, to refer me to the Bosnia and Herzegovina Jamahiriya and then to determine the rules of the game as it fits particular parties at any given moment. Let us see what the law -- what is the law applied by the courts in the Jamahiriya of Bosnia and Herzegovina. What laws? Who is judging? Who is prosecuting? Is it just a branch office of the ICTY in Bosnia and Herzegovina or is the case really to be referred to the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina to be tried according to the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or rather, to the -- or according to the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska? Or would the judgement be delivered by Mr. Paddy Ashdown in some kind of a feudal decree summarily, as he has already done in Republika Srpska? Will I be tried by foreign judges or by Ustasha Mujahedin judges? If I will be tried by Ustasha Mujahedin judges, how can you even think that I would be given a fair trial?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stankovic, I have given you an opportunity to address the Court --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please do not interrupt me because I am about to get to the key issue, the argument in the case. Please allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stankovic, I said one thing to you, that is: Mind your language. Therefore, if you want to refer -- if you want to refer -- your microphone is off, Mr. Stankovic. If you want to refer -- Mr. Stankovic, no one hears you. If you -- I just want to give you the following guidance: If you want to refer -- Mr. Stankovic, now you stop speaking or you're removed. Mr. Stankovic, last warning. The only thing I wanted to say to you, that if you wanted to refer to other groups or ethnicities -- Mr. Stankovic, you'll be removed out of the courtroom. Gentlemen, would you please remove Mr. Stankovic from the courtroom. He'll have an opportunity to hear what's said. Could I ask the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if he would like to know what has been said, then an application could be made for an audio tape of the remainder of this hearing. Well, it's now time for further questions by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one question. Madam Kreso, I'd like to be clear whether I understand you correctly when you said that chapter 17 of the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina will apply to this case. I understand that based on your assertion is that what is alleged in the indictment constituted a crime already then by the -- by then-existing law, but current law of yours is more lenient so that's the base of the application of the current law. Am I correct in understanding so?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRESO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I quoted chapter 17, which lists crimes against humanity and values protected by the international law, I did so to support my claim that the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina is the only court that has jurisdiction to try such cases. I did not go into the length that this law was actually in force. My learned colleague Ms. Lauth actually spoke about that. What I wanted to stress is that the court where the crime was committed is not the only court that has territorial jurisdiction, but one has to take into account the subject matter jurisdiction. No court in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Republika Srpska, Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and district of Brcko has jurisdiction to try such cases. The only court that has been given subject matter jurisdiction to try those cases is the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. I understand that but I'm interested in the substantive law, what law should be applied. You are saying that Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina enacted in 2003 should be applied. In earlier submission you said that there's no need for the international law to be applied in this case, but according to Criminal Code of Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia existed at the time and then -- so what is alleged in the indictment is punishable already but the current law is more lenient, so that's the base, you can apply the current law, as I understand it. But my question is: Why not Criminal Code of Republika Srpska? That's the crux of my question. Could you address the matter, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRESO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Criminal Code of Republika Srpska, which has also been enacted in the past year, does not provide for the Prosecution of those criminal offences. It simply does not contain such provisions because the Prosecution of such cases has been entrusted to the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is the only court that has jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So current Criminal Code of Republika Srpska does not contain those provisions. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRESO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it does not contain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me to add something to what Madam President of the court of BH said. I will ask just one question: What do the cantonal or district courts prosecute in terms of war crimes? It is quite true that war -- that the crimes described in chapter 17 of the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina do not exist in the Criminal Codes of the two entities, but cantonal and district courts do have jurisdiction to prosecute war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is quite true what my colleague Mr. Radovic said. It is quite true that before district and cantonal courts proceedings are underway for war crimes. The court of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the prosecutor's office of Bosnia and Herzegovina at this point simply does not have the capacity to try all the cases that are pending under the rules of the road before various courts and that were sent to the ICTY for review. It is true that there are grounds for suspicion that war crimes have been committed against over 10.000 cases, but the criteria that applied was the sensitivity of each case. There are three -- two categories: Highly sensitive and sensitive cases. Every war crime case must come to the state prosecutor's office of Bosnia and Herzegovina where it is reviewed. If it is determined that a case is of a sensitive nature, it is returned to the cantonal or district court. If a case is determined to be very highly sensitive, then the prosecutor's office of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina keeps it and will prosecute it, but this case on the Rule 11 bis is not one of those cases. According to the law on transfer of cases, this case is directly transferred to the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the court and the prosecutor's office, and cannot be transferred to any other case [as interpreted] but only can be tried before the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Let me just very briefly say something. If Your Honours decide to refer this case with an indictment that was already confirmed to the prosecutor's office of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, according to the law on criminal procedure, the prosecutor's office must adapt the indictment, but this takes a very short time. I think that this will not take a long time; my learned colleague knows that full well. All you need to do is list the name of the court, the personal details of the accused, the factual description of the act, the legal qualification of the act, the evidence, and supporting material, and the case proceeds to trial automatically. Let me, if I may, briefly say something about the topic that was discussed yesterday. The current law in Bosnia and Herzegovina is one of the strictest laws when it comes to detention. The longest period in detention that a person can spend in detention is six months from the date of the confirmation of the indictment. If within six months an indictment is not issued, a suspect must be released. Once an indictment has been issued, the trial judgement must be delivered within one year. If that is not the case, the accused must be released. The appellate judgement must be delivered within six months from the trial judgement, if not ... and so on. That is all I had to say at this point. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have the following question to you, and I'm addressing both Mr. Radovic and the representatives of the -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I do understand that it was the federal Criminal Code and then in 1992 the states or entities that had declared themselves or behaved as independent adopted then the old text and made it -- well, their own national or domestic code. Since Mr. Radovic is referring to the Republika Srpska Criminal Code of 1992, I think you said it was adopted in April, mid-April 1992. Am I correct, Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the constitution of Republika Srpska of 1992 adopts all the laws of the former SFRY, including the Criminal Code of the SFRY. And this was in force until the enactment of a new law in 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question is the following: Since you both, I would say, took over this same code although it's the -- there's still a bit of a time problem because the indictment goes from April to I think December and this happened in April, as far as I understand, I think you said the 11th of April, would that mean that on from that moment although under a different name the same laws would apply? When were the first amendments relevant for these types of cases? Were they amended in the -- well, within the period of the indictment - that means still in 1992 - or were the first amendments only later? Whoever knows the answer -- whoever knows the answer. Yes, Ms. Lauth.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAUTH
utterances.text: There were later amendments, actually, later codes adopted in both the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as in the RS. My understanding is that there was a separate Criminal Code adopted in the Federation in 1998 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me just be quite clear. I just want to know whether it makes any difference at all whether in 1992 in the indictment period whether the Republika Srpska code would be applied and, apart from that, what kind of problems that might cause the courts, but the substantive law would be exactly the same under the Republika Srpska code and under the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAUTH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Radovic, you would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree. These are the same provisions, the Republika Srpska and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, both adopted the former Criminal Code of the former SFRY. The Defence asserts that in the case of Mr. Stankovic only Article 142 of the former Criminal Code of the SFRY can apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I then ask the representatives of the government: Would you consider that -- I know that you take the position that the 2003 Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be applicable law, including the latest amendments as attached. Would you agree that if the old code would apply - we now know it makes no difference Republika Srpska or BiH - that the behaviour would fall within the scope of Article 142?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAUTH
utterances.text: Just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're a little reluctant to make that without having beforehand made all the comparisons between the code and the current indictment that the OTP has prepared. But we do think that war crimes sections from the code of the former Yugoslavia would be applicable if the 1992 code from the former Yugoslavia were applied. I'm not going to -- I'm not prepared to say that other sections would not also be applicable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And specifically, again, the sections in the current code for crimes against humanity we view as codifying customary international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we are back to the old problem whether direct applicability of customary international criminal law -- because 142 is about war crimes and not about crimes against humanity. Yes. Then I would have another question. From the agreement you've sent, as it says the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that includes a representative of what is now the entity of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAUTH
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The agreement was signed on 1st of December, 2003, between the High Representative and the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is a three-party Presidency representing all entities in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We'll just confer a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAUTH
utterances.text: All ethnic groups are represented in the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I -- could I then ask who appoints or selects the Serbian representative in the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAUTH
utterances.text: According to Article 5 of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is the parliament of the Republika Srpska, it would be the parliament in the entity that would select or appoint -- nominate the member of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAUTH
utterances.text: If I may refer to the specific provision in the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I take it -- I was just wondering, Mr. Radovic, because that's the reason I put the question. You highly criticised of what -- whether you could create a court or an international court, and I now understand that this is, could I say, kind of a joint enterprise of the entities constituting Bosnia and Herzegovina including Republika Srpska. So when you say we must take distance from that court is something foreign or strange to you, at the same time you're referring to what would be the competent court, applicable law, Republika Srpska law, at the same time I do understand that this court is a result of at least an enterprise of which Republika Srpska participates.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will be brief. The problem is in who can be a judge in any court in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It can only be a citizen of that country. That is regulated by the constitution, and that's where the problem lies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although I think you criticised that for other reasons as well, but you say it's mainly that the court is constituted not only of Bosnia and Herzegovina citizens but also that foreign judges take part in the activities of that court, that makes you reject the option of such a court. Yes. These were my questions at this moment. I'd like to give an opportunity to both parties to make final submissions, but you indicated a few times, Mr. Radovic, that you would not use that right. I don't know whether much should be added to what has been said already. I'll first give the Prosecution, who filed the motion, filed the request, an opportunity to make any final submissions they'd like to make. And if there's any need to respond briefly to that, you still have the opportunity. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will not take very much time. I think we stand on our written submissions and anything supplemental that I indicated earlier on. I will say that because we just received recently the response of counsel opposite, we reject the notion that Trebinje is what is contemplated. It's the state and I think that the correct interpretation of which court is contemplated is -- has been well argued before this Chamber today. There is nothing additional in terms of the laws that we would say we believe the language of one -- effectively the language of "war crimes against civilians" encompasses it -- there are other provisions that should encompass it as well but I would suggest everything has been contained in the initial submission and I think the questions I had asked the Chamber respectfully to inquire of the representatives of the BH have been addressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Somers. Mr. Radovic, before I give you an opportunity to make, if any, further submissions, I'd like to inform you that if you would like to make further written submissions on the basis of the position that has been recently filed by the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then you'll have 14 days to do so. Would you like to make any further submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have nothing to add. The Defence abides by what it stated in its two preliminary submissions of the 22nd of December, 2004, and our submission of the 1st of March, 2005, and what I said at this hearing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Finally, Madam President Kreso, would you like to make any further submissions, then you have an opportunity to do so at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRESO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no new arguments to put forward but I wish to thank this Chamber for its sensitivity in allowing the representatives of the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina to prevent their arguments. I feel that this was useful in more ways than one for both sides and for us, and I might say we are perhaps a little emotional because this is an opportunity not only for the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the prosecutor's office of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as its entire judiciary to demonstrate the extent to which they have caught up with contemporary European legislation, we are a country undergoing transition and the judicial system is one of the mainstays of every country. If you give us a chance by referring this and other cases which you decide as suitable for transferral and in any case you will still have the right to monitor the proceedings and perhaps revoke your decision and have the cases transferred back, you will give us an opportunity to demonstrate not only to the domestic public but also to the international community how much we have achieved in putting our country back on its feet. Thank you for your confidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Madam Kreso. This Chamber fully understands and follows with great attention all the developments in the states of the former Yugoslavia. And I would say it's quite understandable that if you have made such efforts to adapt your legal system to the difficult task of trying international crimes, I can imagine that if there are still cases to be tried, that after having made such efforts and I think the true is same for other states in the former Yugoslavia, but if one wants to show that these efforts and preparations have not been for nothing; the Chamber understands that. This ends this hearing, although not completely in the case against Mr. Stankovic. Although, Madam Kreso, we'd like -- the Chamber would like to thank you for having provided the Chamber with the information we asked for, but there is still a Status Conference in this case. We'll have a break of five minutes. Mr. Radovic, if there would be a possibility for you to meet with your client, you can tell him that he's welcome at the Status Conference to follow and that I'll apply the same rule and that is: He's allowed to speak. If he uses offensive language, if he is refraining -- if he's insulting whoever it is, then as far as his presence is concerned, the Status Conference will be rather short. If he, however, would like to address me in a reasonable way, I'll give him an opportunity to do so. So I'll instruct the security to make him ready for an appearance, but perhaps you pass already this message to him. We'll adjourn for five minutes.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.42 p.m.
